lessons.title: Checking requirements before accepting a reservation
lessons.reading: よやくまえのかくにんとわかりやすいあんない

objectives.text: Match the guest’s requirements with room availability before confirming a booking.
Explain prices, room types, packages and local information as distinct subjects.

sections.title: How front-desk duties connect
sections.body: The front desk does more than hand over a key on arrival. It connects reservation handling, arrival formalities, assistance during the stay and payment on departure. If a request received when booking is not passed to the arrival team, the guest must explain it again. Consider which stage of the stay each enquiry concerns. Your language and manner also affect the impression of the whole property.

sections.title: Check availability before answering
sections.body: For enquiries by telephone, email or website, first establish the requested dates and check whether a room can be offered then. Available rooms are called kūshitsu; a property with no rooms available is manshitsu. Never confirm a booking merely because you remember there being space yesterday. Distinguish receiving a request from confirming that it can be accepted. Changes and cancellations are also part of reservation management, so use current records.

sections.title: Explain the price together with the conditions
sections.body: Guests need more than the displayed price. Explain what is included in the accommodation charge and what costs extra. Service charges, accommodation tax and bathing tax can depend on the property and location. Check the property’s information rather than assuming that every charge applies or has the same amount. Confirm arrival and departure times, room types, and packages including meals or additional services. Single and twin rooms have different bed arrangements; describe the arrangement instead of relying on the name alone.

sections.title: Give accurate information about the property and area
sections.body: Views from rooms, the food served, and local culture and events can all influence a booking. Instead of giving every guest a long identical explanation, ask about priorities—for example, whether views or food matter more—and then organise the relevant information. Check anything you do not know before answering. The conversations here are practice examples, not promises that a particular property always provides these services.

terms.meaning: A guest room that is available for sale.
A situation with no rooms available for sale.
A product combining accommodation with conditions such as meals.
Work involving reservation acceptance, changes and cancellations.

example.situation: A guest calls the fictional Aoba Hotel: “Two of us would like to stay on the 12th of next month. Is breakfast included?”
steps: Confirm the date and number of guests, then check room availability for that date.
Check the room that can be offered and the conditions of the breakfast-inclusive package.
Explain separately what the room charge includes, any extra charges and the hours of use.
Check that the conditions you explained match the guest’s wishes.

practice.prompt: What misunderstandings could result if you end the call after stating only the room price? List five items to explain.
expectedPoints: Whether meals and additional services are included
Conditions for service charges, taxes and similar items

questions.prompt: What should you check first when receiving a booking enquiry?
choices: Whether a room can be provided on the requested date
The employee’s favourite sightseeing destination
Only last year’s average price
The guest’s employer’s sales
questions.explanation: Whether the reservation can be accepted depends on availability for the requested date.

questions.prompt: Which explanation of a breakfast-inclusive package is most appropriate?
choices: Say all additional services are also free
Check and explain the displayed price, inclusions and additional charges
Say there is no need to check availability
Say breakfast hours are the same at every property
questions.explanation: Explain the package’s scope specifically and avoid ambiguity about prices or conditions.

questions.prompt: Which description is appropriate when confirming a twin room?
choices: A room that always includes two meals
A room that must be booked for two nights
A room with two beds
A room with one single bed
questions.explanation: Twin refers to a room arrangement with two beds. Meals and number of nights are separate conditions.

questions.prompt: A guest asks about a local event, but you do not know its dates. What should you do?
choices: Give last year’s dates as this year’s
Say every event runs daily
Refuse to answer because it is unrelated to booking
Check reliable information before explaining
questions.explanation: Local information is also part of assistance. Do not guess about details you do not know.

questions.prompt: Which best describes the front desk’s role?
choices: Connect information from booking through departure
Stop accepting enquiries once the key is handed over
Hold no information except payment details
Have no need to coordinate with housekeeping
questions.explanation: The front desk is a contact point for reservation, arrival, stay and departure, connecting information between them.

illustration.caption: Check the requested date, room availability and pricing conditions before offering a reservation.
illustration.alt: A diagram comparing room inventory over two dates with meal-inclusive and room-only packages.

lessons.title: Organising reservation details and handling changes accurately
lessons.reading: よやくじょうほうをととのえ、へんこうをまちがえずにあつかう

objectives.text: Obtain and handle the reservation information needed to prepare for arrival.
Identify the booking and check cancellation conditions and requested changes.

sections.title: Collect the essential booking details
sections.body: When accepting a reservation, confirm the stay date, the booking guest’s name, contact details and number of guests. A phone number or email address may also be needed to contact the guest about the reservation later. Guests can have similar names, so match a name with dates and other details when checking a record. Manage the confirmed information using the property’s procedures and do not show or disclose it to unrelated people.

sections.title: Use information to prepare for arrival and meals
sections.body: Asking how the guest will travel and when they expect to arrive helps prepare the welcome and arrival arrangements. Food-allergy information must be handed over accurately to the team providing meals. Merely asking a question does not complete the task: decide what needs checking and what the responsible team needs to know. Checking contact information in advance can also help prevent no-shows, where a guest fails to arrive without notice. Possessing contact details alone does not guarantee arrival.

sections.title: Identify the booking before changing it or answering
sections.body: Whether the caller wants different dates or is asking about an item forgotten after departure, first confirm the stay date and booking name to find the relevant record. Changing the first record with the same surname is risky. Compare the request with the original booking and identify exactly what must be adjusted before acting. The same principle applies whether the booking originated by phone, email or website.

sections.title: Check cancellation conditions before explaining charges
sections.body: Charges for cancellation are checked against the property’s cancellation conditions. At Level 2, also consider the conditions set out in accommodation terms and similar documents. Do not assume that all cancellations use one percentage or that telephone cancellations are free. Rather than memorising a nationwide rate, practise matching the applicable conditions to the booking. Ask the responsible person when a condition is unclear, and do not promise an unverified charge or exemption on the spot.

terms.reading: とうちゃくよていじこく
terms.meaning: The time the guest expects to arrive.
A phone number or similar information used to contact the guest about the booking.
Conditions that apply when a reservation is cancelled.
Failure to arrive for a booking without giving notice.

example.situation: There are two bookings under the surname Tanaka. One guest calls to change the number of guests and discuss meals.
steps: Confirm the stay date and booking name to identify the relevant record.
Compare the original guest count with the requested change.
Organise the meal-related questions and pass them to the responsible team.
Reconfirm the updated details with the guest.

practice.prompt: Create a booking note and group its fields into basic information, arrival preparation, meal preparation and change checks.
expectedPoints: Date, name, number of guests and contact details
Relevant booking, changed fields and applicable conditions

questions.prompt: Two bookings have the same guest name. What should you do?
choices: Change the first record found
Check the stay date and other details to identify the booking
Change both bookings simultaneously
Treat them as one booking because the names match
questions.explanation: Do not identify a reservation by name alone. Match dates and other details to prevent changes to the wrong booking.

questions.prompt: Why is it appropriate to ask the travel method and expected arrival time?
choices: To always charge an extra fee
To change the sightseeing destination without permission
To prepare arrival arrangements
To publish the schedule to other people
questions.explanation: Arrival information helps the property prepare to receive the guest.

questions.prompt: What is appropriate when handling cancellation?
choices: Charge a nationwide standard percentage
Waive all fees for telephone cancellations
Charge without identifying the booking
Check the relevant booking and applicable cancellation conditions
questions.explanation: Identify the booking and the property’s applicable conditions before acting.

questions.prompt: How should you handle contact details obtained during booking?
choices: Manage them according to the property’s procedures
Show them to unrelated guests
Use them freely for private advertising
Display them publicly at reception
questions.explanation: Contact details are personal information and require appropriate management.

questions.prompt: After asking about food allergies, what should you do?
choices: Do not inform the meal team
Organise the information accurately and use it for meal preparation
Immediately promise that every request can be accommodated
Do not record anything until arrival
questions.explanation: Use the information for preparation and coordination with the responsible team.

illustration.caption: Booking notes support identification, arrival arrangements and meal preparation.
illustration.alt: A diagram passing a booking note with dates, name, contacts, guest count, travel, arrival time and allergies to the relevant teams.

lessons.title: Arrival checks and explaining the property
lessons.reading: とうちゃくじのかくにんとかんないあんない

objectives.text: Welcome guests with a clean appearance and courteous manner.
Confirm the booking, hand over the key and explain facilities and escape routes.

sections.title: Prepare your arrival service
sections.body: Arriving guests form an impression from the front desk’s appearance, posture and way of speaking. Keep a clean appearance, a composed posture and use clear, courteous language. Check-in is a sequence: confirm the reservation, complete necessary formalities and help the guest start using the room. Prioritising handing over the key quickly while skipping checks can create confusion later in the stay.

sections.title: Match the booking and its contents
sections.body: Ask the guest’s name and check whether a reservation exists. Even after finding a record, check whether the guest count and booked package match the guest’s understanding. Do not assume that a booking removes the need for confirmation. Discover discrepancies early—for example, a guest expecting breakfast when the booking is room-only. If you cannot find the reservation, continue checking rather than treating a similarly named booking as theirs.

sections.title: Hand over the key and explain how to use the property
sections.body: After confirming the booking and completing necessary checks, hand over the key for the assigned room. Explain not only the route to the room but also the locations and opening hours of dining areas and available facilities. Hours vary by property. Do not turn general examples in a manual into nationwide compulsory times. Check and explain the times that apply at this property.

sections.title: Do not omit safety information
sections.body: Explain the emergency exits and evacuation routes used during a fire or disaster clearly and reliably, separately from everyday facility information. Rushing through the restaurant and emergency-exit directions together may not help the guest understand. Practise showing locations relative to the room on a floor plan. Diagrams in this course are for explanation practice; use the actual property’s confirmed routes and instructions. Passport and guest-register procedures must be checked by their scope. MHLW guidance addresses passport presentation and copying for foreign nationals without an address in Japan; foreign nationality alone does not make the same requirement apply to everyone. The Level 2 lesson on individual needs explains this further.

terms.meaning: Keeping clothing and appearance presentable out of consideration for others.
The conditions booked, such as guest count and package.
An exit used to evacuate outside in an emergency.
A route used to move to a safe place.

example.situation: A first-time guest is concerned about where breakfast is served and tomorrow’s departure time.
steps: Welcome the guest calmly and match their name and booking details.
Confirm the number of guests and package, and complete the necessary formalities.
Hand over the key and explain the room, breakfast venue and opening hours.
Use the floor plan to explain emergency exits and evacuation routes.

practice.prompt: Practise a reception explanation covering the room route, facility hours, departure time and emergency exits. Clearly identify any invented property conditions as practice settings.
expectedPoints: Do not describe example times as nationwide rules

questions.prompt: Which combination should be checked at check-in?
choices: Only the guest’s hobbies
Only the employee’s length of service
Booking existence, name, guest count and package
Only nearby properties’ sales
questions.explanation: Confirm that a booking exists and match the name, guest count and package.

questions.prompt: Which explanation is appropriate when handing over the key?
choices: Say only the room number very quickly
Say facility hours are identical everywhere
Omit evacuation information unless asked
Explain the room route, facility locations and hours, and emergency exits
questions.explanation: Handing over the key includes guidance so that the guest can use the room and property with confidence.

questions.prompt: The manual gives typical check-out times. What should you do in practice?
choices: Check and explain this property’s own time
Always use one nationwide time
Do not explain the time
Let each arriving guest freely decide it
questions.explanation: Times differ between properties. General examples are not uniform rules.

questions.prompt: Which approach to welcoming guests is appropriate?
choices: Appearance is enough; language does not matter
Prepare a clean appearance, correct posture and courteous language
Skip all checks when busy
A booked guest needs no greeting
questions.explanation: Appearance, posture and language all affect the check-in impression.

questions.prompt: The reservation is room-only, but the guest expects breakfast. What should you do?
choices: Hand over the key without explanation
Immediately decide it is not their booking
Check and explain the difference between the record and the guest’s expectation
Confirm additions without permission
questions.explanation: Matching booking details helps detect misunderstandings early.

illustration.caption: After checking the booking, use the key and floor plan to explain locations, hours and escape routes.
illustration.alt: A practice floor plan showing reception, the room and breakfast area, and distinguishing normal movement from the escape route.

lessons.title: Handling requests during a stay and coordinating teams
lessons.reading: たいざいちゅうのいらいとぶもんのれんけい

objectives.text: Repeat telephone requests to confirm them and coordinate with the relevant team.
Obtain the guest’s permission before entering their room.

sections.title: Understand teams so you can handle enquiries
sections.body: Guests may ask about more than the property itself, including nearby shops and facilities, so prepare information about both the property and its surroundings. To know whether rooms and equipment are ready and staff are in position, the front desk also needs to understand other teams’ work. Think about which department should confirm each point so that a request does not stall because nobody knows who handles it. In smaller properties, one person may cover several duties.

sections.title: The roles of key teams
sections.body: A doorman welcomes guests at the entrance, directs them to reception and sees them off. Housekeepers clean and prepare amenities. In ryokan, nakai staff help with the stay, including showing guests to rooms and serving meals. The restaurant team serves food. A concierge specialises in information and arrangements inside and outside the property; the front desk may also perform this role. Learn not just job titles but where each request should go.

sections.title: Confirm what you hear on the telephone
sections.body: On internal calls too, speak clearly and at a pace the guest can follow. When receiving a room-service order, repeat it to check that your understanding matches the guest’s. Never guess an unclear item and turn it into an order. At the end of the conversation, practise waiting until the guest has finished and hung up before ending the call yourself. Check both telephone courtesy and the accuracy of the request separately.

sections.title: Obtain permission before entering a guest room
sections.body: Even when delivering requested amenities or food, the request does not grant unrestricted entry. Announce your arrival by knocking or ringing, then enter after receiving permission from the guest. Do not skip permission because you cannot hear a response, are carrying many items or are in a hurry. This lesson covers ordinary service requests. Disasters and emergencies are different situations handled under the property’s procedures and responsible staff’s decisions.

terms.meaning: Repeating what you heard to confirm it.
A room used by a guest for their stay.
A ryokan role involving room guidance, meal service and other assistance.
Taking responsibility for more than one role.

example.situation: A guest calls to request extra towels and order drinks.
steps: Speak clearly and repeat the request to confirm it.
Identify the amenities and food-service teams and coordinate the request.
Knock or otherwise announce your arrival when delivering.
Confirm the guest’s permission before entering.

practice.prompt: Create one example request for each: doorman, housekeeper, nakai, restaurant and concierge.
expectedPoints: Room guidance and meals in a ryokan
Information and arrangements inside and outside the property

questions.prompt: You cannot clearly hear a room-service order. What should you do?
choices: Guess and tell the kitchen
Use the previous order
End the call without checking
Ask again and repeat the order
questions.explanation: Confirm the content before passing it to the responsible team.

questions.prompt: You are delivering extra amenities to a guest room. What should you do before entering?
choices: Knock or ring and obtain permission to enter
Enter silently because delivery was requested
Enter freely once you reach the room
Enter immediately even without a reply
questions.explanation: A delivery request is not the same as permission to enter.

questions.prompt: Which team is closely involved in cleaning and preparing amenities?
choices: Doormen
Housekeepers
Only the cashier
The booking distributor
questions.explanation: Housekeepers handle not only cleaning but also preparing amenities.

questions.prompt: Which role specialises in information and arrangements inside and outside the property?
choices: Cook
Cashier
Concierge
Equipment manufacturer
questions.explanation: Concierges provide information and make arrangements; the front desk may also cover this role in a smaller property.

questions.prompt: What is the usual courteous way to end a call with a guest?
choices: Hang up during order confirmation
Hang up first for your own convenience
Hang up while the guest is speaking
Wait until the guest hangs up, then end the call
questions.explanation: Do not cut the guest off; confirm that the conversation has ended.

illustration.caption: Confirm requests, pass them to the responsible team, and check permission at the guest-room door.
illustration.alt: A diagram routing a telephone request through reception to amenities and food-service staff, with permission checked at the room door.

lessons.title: Checking charges and settling payment before departure
lessons.reading: しゅっぱつまえのめいさいかくにんとせいさん

objectives.text: Separate accommodation charges from additional in-house use when checking the bill.
Understand the sequence of explanation, payment confirmation and receipt.

sections.title: Accuracy and consideration for departure plans
sections.body: Check-out completes the formalities and payment for a stay. For a guest in a hurry, organise the necessary checks and work smoothly rather than skipping the amount check. Delays may affect onward travel. However, prioritising speed alone can cause billing errors and take even more time to correct. Decide what needs checking before proceeding.

sections.title: Separate package inclusions from additional use
sections.body: Confirm drinks, room service, massage and similar services used during the stay that are not included in the package. Match the package conditions against usage records so that included items are not charged twice. Checking with the bill is often clearer than asking only whether the guest used anything. These services are examples, not offerings available at every property.

sections.title: Show the itemised bill before receiving payment
sections.body: Present an itemised bill covering accommodation, additional use, service charges and applicable taxes, and explain the charges. Whatever the payment method, check it against the amount billed. Handle the receipt after receiving payment. The Level 2 manual explains issuing and handing over a receipt unless the guest says it is unnecessary. In practice, distinguish presenting the breakdown, confirming payment and providing the receipt.

sections.title: Do not confuse service charges with tips
sections.body: Japanese accommodation generally does not assume tipping, while a service charge may be included in the room price or shown separately. Do not treat a service charge as a tip and explain it twice. Accommodation and bathing taxes depend on local government and property conditions. Check what actually applies to this guest’s bill rather than presenting one tax rate or set of charges as universal.

terms.meaning: Checking charges and completing payment.

terms.reading: せいきゅうめいさいしょ
terms.meaning: A document showing the breakdown of the amount charged.
A document acknowledging receipt of payment.
Services and similar items used within the property in addition to accommodation.

example.situation: A practice bill lists accommodation of ¥12,000, drinks outside the package of ¥600 and a separately shown service charge of ¥1,200. No tax is assigned in this exercise.
steps: Check that the drinks are outside the package and match the usage record.
Show the breakdown of accommodation, drinks and service charge.
Confirm the total of ¥13,800 and receive payment.
Explain the receipt provided after payment.

practice.prompt: You discover that the drinks on this practice bill were actually included in the package. What should you recheck and correct?
expectedPoints: Match package conditions and usage records
Present the corrected breakdown and total
Do not rush payment before checking

questions.prompt: Why check additional in-house use at check-out?
choices: To charge every service twice
To include package-excluded usage in settlement
To always increase the accommodation charge
To avoid providing a receipt
questions.explanation: Check whether additional use occurred and what it involved so the bill is accurate.

questions.prompt: What should be shown before payment?
choices: Other guests’ personal information
The employee’s rota
An itemised breakdown of the charges
Only an unverified estimate
questions.explanation: Present the breakdown so that the guest can check the charges.

questions.prompt: What is the total of ¥12,000, ¥600 and ¥1,200 on the practice bill?
questions.explanation: 12,000 + 600 + 1,200 = 13,800. This exercise does not assign taxes or other charges.

questions.prompt: Which understanding of a service charge is correct?
choices: It may be included in the room price or shown separately
It is one fixed amount nationwide
It is always the same as a tip
It never exists in Japanese accommodation
questions.explanation: The manual distinguishes service charges included in accommodation from those billed separately.

questions.prompt: How should you assist a guest in a hurry to leave?
choices: Skip every amount check
Organise necessary checks and proceed accurately and smoothly
Charge extra without checking usage records
Do not show the breakdown
questions.explanation: Consider both efficiency and accuracy.

illustration.caption: Separate included and additional services, then move from bill confirmation to payment and receipt.
illustration.alt: A practice itemised bill with accommodation, drinks and service charge on separate lines, followed by a receipt issued after payment.

lessons.title: Resolving overlapping bookings and handing over calls
lessons.reading: よやくがかさなったときのちょうせいとでんわのひきつぎ

objectives.text: Organise and hand over information when accommodation cannot be provided or the responsible employee is unavailable.

sections.title: Separate the causes of excess bookings
sections.body: At Level 2, analyse why bookings exceed available rooms. Overbooking is a sales approach that accepts more reservations than the total number of rooms in anticipation of some cancellations or no-shows. Double booking is overlapping reservations for the same room arising from reservation-system or management errors. Do not look only at the outcome of insufficient rooms: distinguish a planned sales decision from a recording or processing error. This does not authorise a new employee to overbook on their own.

sections.title: When a room cannot be provided
sections.body: If overbooking remains unresolved or duplicate reservations prevent accommodation, avoid hiding the problem until the guest arrives. When advance contact is possible, contact the guest, apologise and arrange an alternative room at a nearby property. Organise your inventory, affected bookings, contact status and alternative availability, and coordinate with the responsible manager. Merely naming another property is not enough; confirm that an actual room can be provided.

sections.title: Reservation staff and product knowledge
sections.body: Staff who handle bookings by telephone or online are called reservation staff. They need to understand not only prices but hours, room arrangements, meal and optional services, views, food and local information. The Level 2 manual also mentions day use, where rooms or facilities are used during the day without an overnight stay. Do not assume overnight stays or meal inclusions; check the scope and conditions of the product sold.

sections.title: Manage holds and unavailable staff
sections.body: If a call transfer requires a long hold, return to the line and explain the situation. If the responsible employee is unavailable, apologise that you cannot connect the caller immediately. Handle the matter yourself if it is within your ability, but do not assert an answer that only that employee can confirm. Give confirmed information such as when the employee can respond, ask whether a callback is needed, and briefly record the contact details and reason for calling. Aim for a handover that avoids making the caller repeat everything.

terms.meaning: Reservations overlapping for the same room or similar inventory.
A room arranged instead when the originally planned room cannot be provided.
Keeping a caller connected while they wait temporarily.
Calling back someone who contacted the property earlier.

example.situation: An inventory-management error has placed two bookings in one room. One party has not yet set out, and the manager is on another call.
steps: Distinguish a planned sales decision from a management error and identify the overlapping bookings.
Tell the manager the situation and affected reservations, and arrange an alternative room.
Contact the guests who can be reached before arrival and apologise with an explanation.
Do not leave the call on hold without an update; explain progress and how contact will continue.

practice.prompt: Create a response note with four fields: cause, explanation to the guest, alternative arrangements and call handover.
expectedPoints: Planned excess bookings or management error
Advance explanation and apology when contact is possible
Arrange a real available room at another property
Callback need, contacts and purpose of call

questions.prompt: What is accepting more reservations than total rooms in anticipation of cancellations called?
choices: Only double booking
Check-out
Overbooking
Housekeeping
questions.explanation: Distinguish planned excess reservations from duplication due to processing errors.

questions.prompt: A management error created two bookings for one room. What should you do?
choices: Wait for arrival without informing the guests
Delete the record to conceal the problem
Do not check alternative availability
Coordinate with the manager and, where possible, contact and apologise in advance and arrange an alternative room
questions.explanation: Organise the accommodation problem and connect guest communication with actual alternative arrangements.

questions.prompt: A hold is likely to become lengthy. What is appropriate?
choices: Return to the call and explain progress
Leave the caller until they disconnect
Hang up without explanation
Transfer without learning the purpose
questions.explanation: A long hold requires an interim update.

questions.prompt: Only the unavailable employee can answer the question. What should you do?
choices: Promise an answer even though you do not know
Explain when they can respond and check callback needs, contacts and the purpose
Say contact details are unnecessary
End the conversation because the employee is absent
questions.explanation: Distinguish matters you can handle from those requiring a handover.

questions.prompt: How should reservation staff explain a day-use product?
choices: Promise it always includes an overnight stay
Do not check hours
Distinguish it from overnight accommodation and check usage conditions
Promise that meals are always included
questions.explanation: Check each product’s scope and conditions.

illustration.caption: Identify the cause of overlapping bookings and proceed to advance contact and alternative rooms.
illustration.alt: A diagram showing two reservations for one room, notification to a manager, an apology by phone and availability checks at another property.

lessons.title: Individual arrival needs and guest information
lessons.reading: こべつのとうちゃくたいおうとおきゃくさまじょうほう

objectives.text: Check the scope of guest-register and passport procedures and protect personal information.
Assess arrival assistance for VIPs, upgrades, walk-in guests and guests with disabilities.

sections.title: Check guest-register requirements and scope
sections.body: At check-in, obtain the information needed for the guest register through the property’s formal procedures. The registration card is also called a shukuchō. As the register can support infectious-disease investigation and prevention of unlawful acts, do not leave illegible or incomplete records unaddressed. Check necessary details such as name, address and contact information against current official guidance. Do not rely only on a particular manual edition: check the property’s current form and handling procedures.

sections.title: Do not decide passport handling by nationality alone
sections.body: The original manual can be read as requiring passport copies from all foreign guests, but its scope needs qualification. MHLW guidance addresses recording nationality and passport number, presenting a passport and retaining a copy for foreign nationals who have no address in Japan. Do not apply one procedure to everyone simply because they are foreign nationals. Check whether the conditions apply, including an address in Japan, and consult the responsible person if unsure. Handle personal information strictly within what the work requires.

sections.title: Confirm the guest’s wishes and consent
sections.body: VIPs may need individual reception that protects privacy rather than discussing detailed plans or information in front of other guests. If a guest requests a higher-grade room, explain the additional price and obtain consent before changing the booking. This is called upselling. Merely hearing a request does not authorise a paid change. Check the room you can offer and its conditions, and confirm that your explanation matches the guest’s choice.

sections.title: Walk-ins and accessibility assistance
sections.body: A guest who arrives without a reservation is a walk-in guest. Do not decide solely on the absence of a booking: check whether a room can be sold, and proceed with reception if one is available. Explain accessible facilities to guests with disabilities and ask what assistance they need. People with the same disability do not necessarily want the same support. Match available facilities to the individual’s needs and coordinate with relevant teams.

sections.title: Treat room numbers as guest information
sections.body: Do not immediately disclose a room number to someone other than the guest. Check with the guest and respond within the permission given. Do not substitute your judgment for the guest’s wishes simply because the caller says they are a friend or relative. Registers, booking records, room numbers and individual check-in may seem like separate tasks, but all involve handling only the necessary information with the appropriate people.

terms.reading: しゅくはくしゃめいぼ
terms.meaning: A record used to collect and manage required information about guests.
Understanding an explained matter and agreeing to it.
Offering added value, such as a higher-grade room, to make an additional sale.
Providing an environment that people with physical limitations or disabilities can use more easily.

example.situation: A foreign-national guest with an address in Japan arrives in a wheelchair and asks about a larger room. Later, someone claiming to be a friend asks for the room number.
steps: Do not automatically require a passport copy based on nationality; check the procedure’s scope.
Check available facilities and the guest’s individual support needs.
Explain the upgrade price and make the change after consent.
Obtain the guest’s permission before giving a room number to a third party.

practice.prompt: Organise these four situations and explain the conditions to check, the guest’s choices, team coordination and information protection.
expectedPoints: Scope based on an address in Japan and other applicable conditions

questions.prompt: Which approach to foreign guests’ passport copies is appropriate?
choices: Apply the same rule to all foreign nationals regardless of their address
Decide all conditions based only on a friend’s statement
Always request a copy from every guest regardless of nationality
Check official guidance’s conditions, including whether there is an address in Japan
questions.explanation: The original wording is too broad. Check the scope under current MHLW guidance.

questions.prompt: A guest requests a paid room upgrade. What is the right order?
choices: Explain the additional price, obtain consent and then change the booking
Change first and charge extra without explanation
Change without deciding the price after hearing the request
Treat consent as unnecessary
questions.explanation: Price explanation and consent precede the paid change.

questions.prompt: What is appropriate when assisting a guest who uses a wheelchair?
choices: Decide how to assist without asking
Explain facilities and support the guest according to their situation and needs
Assume all wheelchair users have the same wishes
Skip checks of available facilities
questions.explanation: Match the property’s accessibility provisions with the individual guest’s needs.

questions.prompt: Someone claiming to be a friend asks for the guest’s room number. What should you do?
choices: Tell them immediately because they say they are a friend
Show them the guest register
Check with the guest and obtain permission before responding
Announce the room number over the public-address system
questions.explanation: Check the guest’s consent before handling their room number.

questions.prompt: How should you handle a guest arriving without a reservation?
choices: Always refuse without checking
Give another guest’s room without checking
Promise accommodation before checking availability
Check whether a room is available for sale and provide reception if it is
questions.explanation: A walk-in has no advance reservation. Check availability first.

questions.prompt: Which way of handling the guest register is appropriate?
choices: Record necessary information accurately and manage personal data appropriately because the register also supports infection tracing and similar purposes
Freely disclose reservation details to other guests
Treat the register only as an upgrade price list
Assume the register needs no management once created
questions.explanation: The guest register can support infectious-disease investigations and prevention of unlawful acts, so its personal information requires appropriate management.

illustration.caption: Check individual needs, consent to prices and permission to disclose information separately.
illustration.alt: A diagram showing a wheelchair user receiving facility information at reception, consent to an upgrade price and guest information withheld from a third party.

lessons.title: Front-desk management and handing over lost property
lessons.reading: ふろんとかんりとわすれもののひきつぎ

objectives.text: Organise service, accounting and guest-information controls as management checks.
Store lost property properly and verify unclear deadlines or procedures.

sections.title: Move from individual tasks to a management perspective
sections.body: Managing the front desk means maintaining service quality across the department, not simply being courteous yourself. Inconsistent responses between employees, repeated payment corrections or unattended personal information should be organised as management issues. Check service quality, accounting and guest-information controls separately to identify the area affected. The number of tasks processed quickly is not enough to judge quality.

sections.title: Consider costs and profit as well as revenue
sections.body: Increasing accommodation revenue and securing profit are not the same. Costs such as room-sales commissions, labour and consumables must also be understood. OCC, ADR and RevPAR are KPIs used to understand room sales, but one figure alone does not represent all management performance. This lesson connects the indicator names with management; formulas and numerical comparisons are covered in the relevant planning and publicity lesson.

sections.title: Treat lost property as a storage and verification task
sections.body: When an item is found after check-out, store it and hand it over using the property’s procedures. The practice example records where and when it was found, its characteristics and the employee involved. This is a practice form to prevent omissions, not a legally prescribed nationwide form. When an enquiry arrives, identify the stay by checking the date and booking name. Do not immediately discard found items or give them to someone solely because they claim ownership.

sections.title: Verify deadlines and police procedures before handover
sections.body: The Level 2 manual mentions reporting items with unidentified owners to the police, but that page alone does not specify exact deadlines, property categories or detailed reporting and storage conditions. This course does not invent a universal number of storage days. Learn to have the responsible person check current procedures applicable to the property and pass on necessary records. Do not assume storage deadlines and reporting deadlines are identical, or promise return or disposal dates without verification.

terms.meaning: Managing service so that its standard can be understood and maintained.
Expenditure and other costs required for work or services.
A result understood by deducting costs from revenue.
An item lost or forgotten and no longer in its owner’s possession.

example.situation: A manager notices repeated corrections to bills. On the same day, housekeeping finds a wristwatch in a guest room.
steps: Organise the billing corrections as a management issue.
Check revenue, costs and guest-information management as distinct areas.
Store the found item under property procedures and record the circumstances in the practice form.
If ownership checks or reporting conditions are unclear, consult the responsible person and hand over the information.

practice.prompt: Organise the information employees should report to managers under four headings: service, accounting, guest information and lost property.

questions.prompt: Which combination belongs in front-desk management checks?
choices: Service quality, accounting and guest information
Sales only
Only cleaning-tool colours
Only employees’ preferences
questions.explanation: The manual covers service quality, accounting and guest information as well as revenue structure.

questions.prompt: Why check room-sales commissions and labour costs?
choices: Because revenue alone reveals profit
To understand the structure of revenue, costs and profit
Because all such items are free
Because they have no connection at all to service management
questions.explanation: Costs can change even when sales rise, so profit cannot be assessed without them.

questions.prompt: The source page does not establish a legal deadline for lost property. What should you do?
choices: Invent a convenient number of days
Always use another property’s deadline
Ask the responsible person to check applicable current procedures
Discard the item immediately without checking
questions.explanation: Do not fill gaps in the source with guessed numbers. Verify the applicable conditions.

questions.prompt: Which check is appropriate at the start of a lost-property enquiry?
choices: Promise immediately to hand over the item
Show the caller every guest’s information
Search all rooms without asking a name
Identify the stay using the date and booking name
questions.explanation: Identify the relevant stay before handling the enquiry.

questions.prompt: Which understanding of management indicators is appropriate?
choices: Understand OCC, ADR and RevPAR together with costs and profit
If one indicator rises, no other checks are needed
Costs do not need recording
Revenue always equals profit
questions.explanation: KPIs inform management, while costs and profit also need to be understood.

illustration.caption: Control service, accounting and information, and hand over lost property through records, storage and required procedures.
illustration.alt: A manager’s three control areas and a wristwatch labelled with discovery location and time, placed in a storage box and handed over to the responsible employee.
